title: Crestline Insurance - Private VPC Deployment Discovery
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC2 and security whitepaper
Redwood SE to run latency/cost estimate for 512-token workload
Customer to share VPC CIDR blocks and peering constraints
Schedule follow-up network diagram review with Crestline networking team
Set up 2-node pilot in us-east-1 with private endpoints
action_items: Maya Chen: share security + SOC2 docs and private deployment checklist by 2026-03-06
Daniel Ortiz: provide preliminary latency/cost spreadsheet and recommended instance types by 2026-03-09
Sara Patel: provide VPC CIDR ranges, NAT/egress patterns, and preferred regions by 2026-03-05
topics: Dedicated capacity vs Private deployment tradeoffs
summary: Initial discovery for Crestline Insurance evaluating Redwood Private (VPC) deployment. Main concerns: network connectivity (peering vs PrivateLink), egress/NAT and proxying, region/residency constraints, KMS key custody, and auditing/SOC2. Redwood AE/SE outlined deployment options, integration points, and next steps for a pilot and security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. We have Daniel from our SE team as well. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Tom Chen: Doing good, thanks. Morning from Boston.
[00:12] Sara Patel: Morning, yeah thanks for setting this up.
[00:15] Daniel Ortiz: Hey folks, Daniel here. We'll try to keep this practical, focus on network/infra and security items for Private deployment.
[00:22] Mark Ruiz: Great, Mark here on security. We have a few penciled questions around key management and audit logging.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Awesome, quick agenda: 1) understand your current infra and constraints, 2) go over Redwood Private options (VPC peering, private endpoints), 3) discuss KMS/keys and logs, and 4) next steps. If anything else, flag it.
[00:40] Lena Gomez: Sounds good. I'll try to speak to the platform detail, we run most services in AWS across us-east-1 and eu-west-1.
[00:46] Maya Chen: Perfect. Could you give a high level of how you'd want Redwood to be networked in? VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, or via a transit VPC?
[00:54] Sara Patel: We're leaning away from internet-facing endpoints; private connectivity is non-negotiable for certain workloads. We prefer AWS PrivateLink/private endpoints over peering due to routing control, but we want to understand tradeoffs.
[01:06] Daniel Ortiz: Yep, totally. So quick primer — with Redwood Private we support both VPC peering and PrivateLink-style private endpoints. Peering is simpler but requires route-table management and non-overlapping CIDR. Private endpoints give you more control and less routing surface but add ENIs per AZ.
[01:28] Mark Ruiz: On the ENI side, we need to know about IP usage and limits. We already have tight /20s per environment.
[01:36] Daniel Ortiz: Understood, ENI consumption can be a concern with PrivateLink especially across many AZs. In that case we can size the endpoint subnets carefully or consider peering with NAT gateway egress control. Also, we can run a proxy layer in your VPC to consolidate egress.
[01:52] Tom Chen: Wait can you clarify the proxy option? We prefer a single egress IP for allowlisting partner APIs.
[01:58] Maya Chen: Sure — Redwood can be deployed with a small set of NAT/proxy instances in your VPC that all outbound traffic goes through, so the external IPs are stable. Alternatively, if you use PrivateLink, egress towards external services still happens out of your VPC unless you route otherwise.
[02:14] Lena Gomez: That sounds reasonable. For our networking team, we need to know the minimum required CIDR and how many ENIs per AZ we should expect.
[02:22] Daniel Ortiz: For a typical pilot with two serving nodes per AZ, expect O(5-10) ENIs depending on instance types. Minimum subnet size we recommend /24 per endpoint subnet in each AZ to be safe, but we can get by with smaller ranges for pilot. I'll put exact numbers in the follow-up doc.
[02:40] Mark Ruiz: On encryption, are you supporting customer-managed keys? BYOK?
[02:44] Maya Chen: Yes, we support KMS integration. For Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS — you can bring your own key (BYOK) or use a customer-managed KMS in your account. For Hosted we don't have BYOK.
[02:58] Mark Ruiz: Any HSM or external KMS options? We have a HSM-backed KMS in our environment.
[03:03] Daniel Ortiz: We can integrate with AWS KMS that is HSM-backed. If you have an external HSM we can discuss a connector or using the customer's key material in a supported workflow — we'll capture specifics in the security doc.
[03:15] Sara Patel: Okay that covers keys. On auditing, we need detailed request logs and token-level cost traces for compliance. What retention options exist?
[03:24] Maya Chen: Redwood's Private deployment can push audit logs to your S3/Bucket or to a SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch. Retention is configurable — default is 90 days but enterprise retention tiers can be configured for longer. We'll send the exact formats and sample schemas.
[03:37] Tom Chen: Also SSO — we use Okta and need SAML/SCIM for user provisioning and RBAC.
[03:42] Daniel Ortiz: We support SAML for the Redwood Console and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC maps to Okta groups; we can walk you through claim mapping.
[03:50] Maya Chen: Quick qual question — what's the main workload? Are you primarily embedding search, or are you doing conversational assistants with long contexts?
[03:58] Lena Gomez: Mix of both. Most critical is an assistant for claims intake with roughly 512 token contexts and batch embedding jobs overnight. Latency for inference during claims intake needs to be <250ms p50 ideally.
[04:12] Daniel Ortiz: For 512 token generation, with Dedicated GPU-backed nodes we can usually hit p50 sub-200ms depending on model. If you need sub-100ms we'd look at smaller models or caching. We'll run benchmarks against your workload.
[04:24] Mark Ruiz: Any fallbacks if your primary region is constrained — we operate multi-region, need DR for inference.
[04:31] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, Redwood supports multi-region Private deployments. You can run control plane in one region and data plane in others, or we can replicate endpoints. There are tradeoffs: cross-region KV cache coherency and cold-start latency. For DR we'd recommend active-active in two regions, with model version pinning across both.
[04:49] Sara Patel: Are there constraints on regions? We need eu-west-1 for EMEA data residency and us-east-1 for NA.
[04:56] Maya Chen: We support both regions. For Private we can deploy in eu-west-1 and us-east-1; we just need network connectivity details for each region and any egress policy differences.
[05:06] Tom Chen: Licensing/cost — how is Private priced vs Dedicated?
[05:10] Maya Chen: Private is a licensing + deployment fee plus support tier, whereas Dedicated is reserved capacity in Redwood-managed infra with monthly commit. I'll follow up with a pricing sheet.
[05:18] Lena Gomez: Back to network — what about NAT vs egress through our firewall? We have strict outbound rules.
[05:24] Daniel Ortiz: We can place egress through your firewall. If using PrivateLink, traffic destined for external services still leaves your VPC; you control firewall/NAT. If peering directly to our VPC we can also arrange egress through a transit GW pattern. A diagram will help — we'll request your current network topology.
[05:42] Mark Ruiz: Regarding peering, overlap in CIDR will block peering. We have RFC1918 across many accounts, so this may be a blocker.
[05:50] Maya Chen: If overlapping CIDR is an issue, PrivateLink or a proxy-based approach is usually the fix. We can also work through NAT translation or use a translator VPC.
[05:59] Sara Patel: Are there any required ports/protocols for the Private endpoint?
[06:03] Daniel Ortiz: Standard TLS over 443 for API traffic. For control-plane operations we may need a couple of management endpoints; details will be in the deployment checklist.
[06:14] Tom Chen: Is there a way to test with our own models or do we need Redwood curated models?
[06:20] Maya Chen: For Private you can bring your own model artifacts, as long as they are compatible with our runtime. Many customers bring custom fine-tuned models. We'll share model packaging requirements.
[06:30] Lena Gomez: What's the onboarding timeline for Private deployment? We have internal Q3 requirements.
[06:34] Daniel Ortiz: Typical pilot can be 2-4 weeks to stand up a pilot with our runbook, then 6-8 weeks for a production rollout depending on network approvals and SOC checks. For Q3 that seems doable if we start now.
[06:46] Mark Ruiz: One security-specific: can the audit logs be delivered to our SIEM with PII redaction? We want queryable logs but not sensitive PII stored long-term.
[06:57] Daniel Ortiz: We can pipeline raw logs into your processing tier where you can apply redaction rules before long-term storage. Redwood can also redact sensitive fields at the source if you provide the schema.
[07:09] Sara Patel: We also need to understand who holds keys and the rotation process. If Redwood manages the KMS, how do we ensure rotation meets our policy?
[07:18] Maya Chen: For Private deployments we recommend customer-managed keys. If Redwood manages keys we provide rotation schedules and audit access. But BYOK in your account gives you full rotation control.
[07:29] Tom Chen: Any SOC2 or ISO attestations to share?
[07:32] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share SOC2 Type II and our latest security whitepaper. Those are part of the follow-up.
[07:38] Lena Gomez: Network peering question — does Redwood need a public IP on our VPC?
[07:43] Daniel Ortiz: No, not if you use PrivateLink or peering plus internal endpoints. Public IPs are only needed if you want internet egress directly from our nodes. In Private deployments we recommend no public IPs on nodes.
[07:53] Mark Ruiz: Performance monitoring — how do we instrument latency and cost at token level?
[07:59] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency histograms. For Private we can forward metrics to your metrics stack (Prometheus/Grafana) or push traces to your tracing backend.
[08:10] Sara Patel: Can we see a sample dashboard?
[08:13] Maya Chen: I'll share screenshots and access to a sandbox dashboard.
[08:16] Tom Chen: Are there small gotchas with IPv6? We are IPv4 primary but evaluating IPv6.
[08:22] Daniel Ortiz: We primarily use IPv4 in most customer deployments. IPv6 support is limited in some managed infra; if IPv6 is a hard requirement we'll need to validate in the pilot.
[08:31] Sara Patel: Okay, switching briefly to IAM — we'd like to map service accounts to least-privilege roles for the nodes.
[08:37] Daniel Ortiz: For AWS we use IAM roles attached to EC2/ECS tasks in your account; we'll provide an IAM policy template. You maintain role permissions.
[08:45] Maya Chen: Quick check: are there legal or procurement blockers like data processing agreements or specific PAT clauses we should be aware of?
[08:52] Tom Chen: We need a DPA and a standard data residency clause for EU data. Also we push for contract clause around subprocessing.
[09:00] Maya Chen: Noted — legal will send standard DPA template. We'll highlight Private deployment-specific terms.
[09:06] Lena Gomez: For embedding batch jobs overnight, would you recommend a separate Private endpoint or same cluster?
[09:12] Daniel Ortiz: Typically we recommend separate worker clusters for large async batches to avoid impacting low-latency serving. That can be separated by namespace and instance class.
[09:22] Mark Ruiz: Is there a simple way to throttle or limit token consumption per route?
[09:26] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood provides per-route quotas and rate limits and you can gate by API key or by token budget per project.
[09:34] Sara Patel: Time check — we have about 10 minutes left. Two quick items: 1) we'd like to see the deployment runbook, and 2) we need a concrete pilot proposal.
[09:45] Maya Chen: We'll send both. Pilot proposal will include exact instance sizes, expected latency, cost estimates, and a network diagram.
[09:52] Daniel Ortiz: I'll include an initial latency table: p50/p95 for 256/512 tokens across recommended instance types, and estimated network/ENI counts.
[09:59] Tom Chen: Can we schedule the network diagram review next week? Our network lead is available Wednesday.
[10:04] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll propose Wed 2026-03-11 at 10am ET.
[10:09] Sara Patel: Works for us.
[10:11] Maya Chen: Great. Any final questions?
[10:13] Mark Ruiz: One small one — compliance scans. Do you run vulnerability scans on deployed nodes?
[10:17] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, standard vulnerability scanning and image hardening, and we provide the SBOM for images used in Private deployments.
[10:24] Lena Gomez: That should cover it. Thanks — we'll gather the CIDR info and regions and send by Friday.
[10:30] Maya Chen: Awesome, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and pilot proposal.
[10:36] Tom Chen: Thanks all.
[10:38] End of recording

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings; proper nouns like "KV cache" may appear as "KV cash" in auto-transcript. Artefacts shared: security whitepaper link, deployment checklist, pilot pricing spreadsheet. Links to be shared in follow-up: https://redwood.example.com/security-whitepaper, https://redwood.example.com/private-deploy-checklist, shared pilot spreadsheet (internal link).
